or_6_northwest_face.blurb: One of the bigger walls in the Smith Rock Group at Smith Rock State Park in central Oregon, sitting on the group's northwest side just beyond Asterisk Pass. It holds 27 routes, nearly all of them bolted sport lines with a handful of trad climbs, including at least one long multi-pitch outing. Grades start around 5.5 and run up through 5.11, with the bulk of the lines between 5.8 and 5.11, so there is something for beginners and mid-grade leaders alike. Newer, well-travelled routes share the wall with older relics from earlier eras, and the stone is variable rather than polished, so expect some loose or crumbly sections.

or_west_face.blurb: The best-developed side of the Kangaroo, a thick spire in the Marsupials section of Smith Rock State Park in central Oregon. All 26 routes are sport climbs, and they are steep and demanding: one climb around 5.10, a couple at 5.11, then a heavy cluster of 5.12 and 5.13 with a single 5.14. Many lines are equipped with permanent cable quickdraws. The wall looks over the canal, stays shaded early in the day, catches a steady breeze and offers mountain views. It sees fewer people than the park's busiest hard-sport walls, making it a strong choice for strong sport climbers.
or_west_face.approach: Follow the trail that runs alongside the canal; the wall comes into view along the way.

or_toothpick_wall.blurb: A cliff within the Rocky Butte quarry crag in northeast Portland, Oregon, known for its crack climbing. Of 26 routes, roughly half are top-rope, a bit under half are trad, and just a few are bolted. Grades span from easy through the 5.12 range, but most cluster around 5.9 and 5.11. The wall is described as clean and quiet, and few lines have fixed anchors, so most climbers set top ropes from nearby trees or with their own gear. Because it sits in an urban quarry, watch for broken glass on the ground.

or_monkey_face.blurb: Smith Rock's most famous landmark: a roughly 350-foot freestanding spire above the Crooked River in central Oregon. Its 24 listed climbs mix trad, sport and aid, with a few top-rope lines. Grades stretch from moderate fifth-class up past 5.14, but the weight sits at 5.12, so it rewards strong leaders, while the aid ladders give less experienced parties a way onto the spire. Faces, thin cracks and overhanging arêtes make for exposed, airy climbing. It is windy in cold months and cooler than the rest of the park in summer, and few people actually go up it.

or_bulo_point.blurb: A small, forested crag on the east side of Mt. Hood National Forest, just north of the Badger Creek Wilderness in Wasco County, at roughly 4,700 feet. It has 24 routes, around fourteen of them bolted and about ten trad. Grades run from 5.6 to the low 5.12s, but most are 5.8 through 5.10, which makes it friendly for newer climbers, especially as many lines can be top-roped. A couple of steeper, overhanging faces and some boulder problems add variety. The drive in uses gravel forest roads, and high clearance helps near the end.

or_main_area.blurb: The largest continuous stretch of rock on Cougar Buttress, a quiet crag above Tumalo Creek in central Oregon, at about 5,200 feet. Scree gullies split the buttress, and this section holds the big multi-pitch lines of up to roughly 600 feet. The 24 routes divide into 14 sport and 10 trad climbs. Most fall between 5.10 and 5.11, with a few easier lines in the 5.7 to 5.9 range and a couple of 5.12s. Holds can be questionable, so a helmet and a careful look before committing are advised. Expect little traffic; it suits a locals' weekend more than a destination trip.
